procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 3, 1968, of the Delhi High Court in Civil Writ Petition No. 817 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed a writ petition challenging the power of the Central Government to make nominations for admissions to Maulana Azad Medical College. The High Court dismissed the petition on December 3, 1968. The appellants then filed a petition for review of the judgment, which was dismissed by the High Court on January 27, 1969.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against both the judgment dismissing the writ petition and the order dismissing the review petition. However, the certificate granted by the High Court was limited to the appeal against the original judgment dismissing the writ petition. The Supreme Court noted that the order rejecting the review application was not appealable under Order 47, Rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code, and leave to appeal against that order was not sought under Article 136 of the Constitution. Therefore, the arguments before the Supreme Court were confined to the matters decided by the original judgment of December 3, 1968. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal fails and it is dismissed with no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order of the court rejecting an application for review is appealable.

facts: The appellants filed a petition in the High Court seeking a review of a judgment dated December 3, 1968.
The High Court dismissed this review petition on January 27, 1969.
The appellants then sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against both the original judgment and the order dismissing the review petition.
law: The Court cited Order 47, Rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code.
This rule provides that an order of a court rejecting an application for review is not appealable.
application: The Court applied Order 47, Rule 7 to the appellants' attempt to appeal the dismissal of their review petition.
Because the rule explicitly states that such an order is not appealable, the Court found that this part of the appeal was invalid.

The Court also noted that the correct procedure to challenge the rejection of a review petition would have been to seek special leave from the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution, which the appellants had not done.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that an order rejecting an application for review is not appealable, based on the clear prohibition in Order 47, Rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code.

issue.issue_text: Whether appellants who do not compete for reserved seats have the locus standi to challenge the nominations made to such seats.

facts: The appellants were students who applied for admission to the general, non-reserved seats in a medical college.
They did not apply for or compete for the seats that were reserved for specific categories and filled by nomination by the Central Government.
law: To have 'locus standi' (the legal right to bring a case), a person must have a direct interest in the matter being challenged.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that because the appellants did not compete for the reserved seats, they had no legal right or standing to challenge the nominations made to those specific seats.
The Court also rejected the appellants' argument that if the nominations were improper, the seats should be transferred to the general pool.
It held that this assumption was "wholly unfounded" and that the Central Government was under no obligation to release those seats to the general pool.
While the government could choose to release the seats, it could not be forced to do so at the request of students who were not eligible for the reserved categories in the first place.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appellants did not have the locus standi to challenge the nominations because they were not candidates for the reserved seats and had no legal right to claim them even if the nominations were found to be improper.

issue.issue_text: Whether reserved seats that have not been properly filled up would be thrown open to the general pool.

facts: The appellants were students from the general pool who sought admission to a medical college.
They argued that some nominations made by the Central Government to reserved seats were not in accordance with the rules.
The appellants contended that any reserved seats that were improperly filled should be made available to the general pool of candidates.
law: Students who do not compete for reserved seats have no 'locus standi' (the legal right) to challenge the nominations made to those seats.
There is no legal rule or obligation that requires the government to release improperly filled reserved seats to the general pool.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the appellants, as general pool candidates, were not in competition for the reserved seats.
Because they were not competing for these specific seats, the Court found that the appellants lacked the legal standing to challenge how the nominations were made.
The Court described the appellants' assumption—that improperly filled reserved seats must be thrown open to the general pool—as "wholly unfounded."

The Court clarified that while the Central Government *may* choose to release such seats to the general pool, it "cannot be compelled to do so" at the request of students from non-reserved categories.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the appellants had no legal right to challenge the nominations for reserved seats, and the government was under no obligation to transfer any improperly filled reserved seats to the general pool.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of making a classification, provided it is based on a reasonable basis such as territorial or geographical grounds.

facts: A centrally administered medical college had rules that reserved seats for specific categories of students.

These categories included residents of Union territories (other than Delhi), children of Central Government servants posted abroad, scholars under cultural exchange programs (like the Colombo Plan), and scholars from Jammu & Kashmir.
Appellants, who were denied admission, challenged these reservations, arguing they were discriminatory.
law: The Supreme Court relied on the principle established in *Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar* regarding Article 14 of the Constitution.
Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification.

For a classification to be permissible, it must satisfy two conditions: (i) it must be founded on an intelligible differentia that distinguishes the grouped individuals from others, and (ii) this differentia must have a rational relation to the objective sought to be achieved.

The Court affirmed that deciding the sources for admission is essentially a question of government policy, and it is not for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of a classification, provided it is reasonable.
application: The Court examined each category of reservation to determine if it met the two-pronged test for reasonable classification.

**Union Territories:** The Court found these areas to be comparatively backward and lacking their own medical colleges. Reserving seats for their residents had a rational connection to the objective of providing them with medical education facilities.

**Children of Diplomats:** The Court recognized that these children face significant educational difficulties abroad (language barriers, admission problems). The reservation was a rational way to address this disadvantage.

**Foreign & J&K Scholars:** Admissions for foreign scholars were based on reciprocal cultural and educational arrangements. For Jammu & Kashmir scholars, the reservation was justified by the inadequate medical education facilities within the state.

In each case, the Court concluded that the classification was based on an 'intelligible differentia'—the unique and disadvantageous circumstances of each group—which distinguished them from the general pool of applicants to which the appellants belonged.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the issue, holding that it is not the role of the courts to interfere with the government's method of classification for college admissions, as this is a matter of policy. The Court found that the classification, based on territorial and other grounds, was reasonable because it was founded on an intelligible differentia (the specific needs and disadvantages of each group) that had a rational relationship to the government's objective of providing medical education to them. Therefore, the classification was valid under Article 14.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order of the court rejecting an application for review is appealable.
appellant_arguments: The appellants sought leave to appeal against the original judgment dismissing the writ petition as well as the subsequent order by which their review petition was disposed of, implying they believed the order was appealable.
The appellants attempted to argue points that were raised only at the review stage, such as the legality of nominations based on the application deadline.

arguments.issue_text: Whether appellants who do not compete for reserved seats have the locus standi to challenge the nominations made to such seats.
appellant_arguments: The appellants challenged the power of the Central Government to make nominations and contended that the nominations were contrary to the rules.
They argued that students nominated by the government had obtained lower marks, and if these nominations were excluded, the appellants would be entitled to admission.
respondent_arguments: The appellants did not compete for the reserved seats and therefore had no locus standi (right to bring an action) in the matter of nomination to such seats.

arguments.issue_text: Whether reserved seats that have not been properly filled up would be thrown open to the general pool.
appellant_arguments: If nominations to reserved seats were not in accordance with the rules, such seats must be regarded as not having been properly filled and must be thrown open to the general pool.
respondent_arguments: The Central Government is under no obligation to release improperly filled reserved seats to the general pool.
While the government could release such seats in the larger interest of other candidates, it cannot be compelled to do so at the instance of students from non-reserved categories.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it is for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of making a classification, provided it is based on a reasonable basis such as territorial or geographical grounds.
appellant_arguments: The provisions in the rules for reservation of seats were not based on any reasonable classification and were therefore violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.
The rules also violated clauses (1) and (4) of Article 15 as well as clause (2) of Article 29.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not explicitly state the respondent's arguments on this specific issue, as the court dismissed the challenge on the preliminary ground of locus standi.

cases.case_name: Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar & Others
cases.principle: Article 14 forbids class legislation but not reasonable classification. For a classification to be permissible, it must fulfill two conditions: (i) it must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group, and (ii) the differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A candidate who applies for admission from the general pool does not have the legal standing (locus standi) to challenge nominations made to reserved seats, as they do not compete for those specific seats. Consequently, the government cannot be compelled to release any reserved seats to the general pool, even if those seats are not filled in accordance with the rules. When a classification for reservation is based on a reasonable basis, such as territorial or geographical considerations, courts will not interfere with the manner and method of making that classification.
obiter: The High Court was in error for examining the merits of the nominations to the reserved seats and ordering two of them to be converted to the general pool, as the petitioners lacked the standing to challenge those nominations in the first place.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court held that the Central Government, as the financial authority for the medical college, has the right to establish admission criteria, including reserving seats for specific categories of students. The classification of these reserved seats—for residents of Union territories without medical colleges, children of government servants posted abroad, and others—is a reasonable classification founded on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the object of imparting medical education, and thus does not violate Article 14 of the Constitution. Furthermore, students who apply for the general pool of seats lack the legal standing (locus standi) to challenge the nominations made to these reserved seats, and they cannot compel the government to transfer any improperly filled reserved seats to the general pool.
legal_tests_applied: The test for permissible classification under Article 14, as laid down in Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar & Others, which requires two conditions to be fulfilled: (i) that the classification is founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group and, (ii) that the differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants did not have the locus standi to challenge the nominations made by the Central Government because they did not compete for the reserved seats.

The appellants' contention that improperly filled reserved seats must be thrown open to the general pool was found to be 'wholly unfounded,' as the Central Government is under no legal obligation to release those seats.

The reservation of seats was not violative of Article 14 because the classification of categories (e.g., residents of Union territories, children of government servants abroad) was based on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the object of providing medical education.
The rules did not violate Article 15(1) as they did not discriminate on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
Article 29(2) was not violated as the appellants were not denied admission on any of the grounds mentioned in that article.
why_respondent_won: The Central Government, which bears the financial burden of the college, has the right to lay down the criteria for eligibility and decide from what sources admissions will be made.

The classification of reserved seats was constitutionally valid under Article 14, as it was based on an intelligible differentia (such as the backwardness of Union territories, lack of medical colleges, and difficulties faced by children of diplomats) that had a rational relation to the object of imparting medical education.
The appellants lacked the legal standing to challenge nominations for seats they were not competing for.
The government cannot be compelled to release reserved seats to the general pool at the instance of students from non-reserved categories.
policy_considerations: The determination of admission sources is essentially a question of policy for the government, based on an overall assessment of the needs of residents of particular territories and other categories for whom it is essential to provide medical education facilities.

It is not for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of making a classification, provided the sources for admission are properly classified on a territorial, geographical, or other reasonable basis.
It is necessary to provide medical education facilities for residents of Union territories which are comparatively backward and do not have their own medical colleges.
The children of Central Government servants posted in Indian Missions abroad face significant difficulties in education due to the exigencies of their parents' service, justifying the reservation.
Admissions for foreign scholars are justified by reciprocal arrangements of an educational and cultural nature.
The problems relating to Jammu & Kashmir scholars are of a peculiar nature, and there are inadequate arrangements for medical education within that State.
